subjects.name: Refrigeration Cycle
defs: The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit.
The total rate of heat removal from the conditioned space by a refrigeration system.
The movement of thermal energy from a warmer substance to a cooler substance by conduction, convection, or radiation.
Heat absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature and pressure.
A closed loop process that transfers heat from a low-temperature space to a high-temperature space.
The amount of heat absorbed in the evaporator per unit mass of refrigerant circulated.
Heat that causes a change in temperature of a substance without a change in phase.
A rate of heat removal equal to 12,000 British thermal units per hour.
The ratio of the volume of vapor actually drawn into a compressor to its theoretical displacement.
A vessel on the low side that prevents liquid refrigerant from entering the compressor.
A fixed-length small-diameter tube that creates a pressure drop to meter refrigerant flow.
A component that increases refrigerant pressure and temperature by reducing its volume.
A heat exchanger that rejects heat from hot refrigerant vapor to a cooler medium, causing condensation.
A metering device whose opening is adjusted by a stepper motor in response to sensor signals.
A heat exchanger that absorbs heat into refrigerant, causing liquid to evaporate into vapor.
A device that removes moisture and particulate contaminants from the refrigerant circuit.
The tubing that carries liquid refrigerant from the condenser outlet to the metering device.
A component that restricts refrigerant flow, creating a pressure drop between high and low sides.
A device that removes lubricating oil from hot discharge gas and returns it to the compressor crankcase.
A vessel on the high side that stores liquid refrigerant between the condenser and metering device.
A transparent window in the liquid line used to observe refrigerant flow and moisture indication.
The tubing that carries low-pressure refrigerant vapor from the evaporator outlet back to the compressor.
A metering device that modulates refrigerant flow based on evaporator outlet superheat.
A refrigerant blend that evaporates and condenses at a constant temperature like a pure compound.
A relative measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps compared to carbon dioxide over a time horizon.
A relative measure of a substance's ability to destroy stratospheric ozone compared to R-11.
A hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant used in automotive and some commercial refrigeration applications.
A hydrochlorofluorocarbon refrigerant phased out in many applications due to ozone depletion potential.
A near-azeotropic hydrofluorocarbon blend refrigerant commonly used in residential air conditioning.
A working fluid that changes phase to absorb and release heat in a refrigeration cycle.
Lubricant circulated with refrigerant that protects the compressor and seals internal clearances.
A refrigerant blend whose components evaporate and condense at different temperatures, creating a temperature glide.
The phase change of a vapor to liquid by rejecting heat, occurring in the condenser.
The phase change of a liquid to vapor by absorbing heat, occurring in the evaporator.
Vapor that forms when liquid refrigerant pressure drops abruptly through the metering device.
The correlation showing how a refrigerant's saturation pressure and temperature change together.
The ratio of absolute discharge pressure to absolute suction pressure in a compressor.
The refrigerant pressure in the high side at the compressor discharge outlet.
A reversing valve that changes refrigerant direction to switch a heat pump between heating and cooling modes.
The heat added to refrigerant vapor by mechanical work during compression.
The portion of a refrigeration system operating at condenser pressure between compressor discharge and metering device inlet.
The portion of a refrigeration system operating at evaporator pressure between metering device outlet and compressor suction.
A refrigeration system operating as a heat pump by reversing refrigerant flow to heat the conditioned space.
The refrigerant pressure in the low side at the compressor suction inlet.
The sum of refrigeration effect and heat of compression rejected by the condenser.

subjects.name: Superheat and Subcooling
defs: Saturation temperature of refrigerant in the condenser at a given pressure.
Saturation temperature of refrigerant in the evaporator at a given pressure.
Refrigerant liquid at saturation temperature and pressure with no vapor present.
Refrigerant existing as a mixture of liquid and vapor in equilibrium at saturation conditions.
Refrigerant vapor at saturation temperature and pressure with no liquid present.
The pressure at which a refrigerant changes phase at a given temperature.
The temperature at which a refrigerant changes phase at a given pressure.
A saturated mixture containing both liquid and vapor refrigerant.
Difference between compressor discharge temperature and condensing saturation temperature.
Temperature difference between suction line and evaporator saturation temperature.
The amount by which refrigerant vapor temperature exceeds its saturation temperature.
Refrigerant vapor heated above its saturation temperature at a given pressure.
Superheat measured at the evaporator outlet comparing suction line temperature to saturation.
Superheat in the evaporator that contributes to sensible heat absorption of refrigerant.
Temperature difference between condensing saturation and actual liquid line temperature.
Refrigerant liquid cooled below its saturation temperature at a given pressure.
The amount by which refrigerant liquid temperature falls below its saturation temperature.
Subcooling measured at the condenser outlet comparing liquid line temperature to saturation.
Difference between condensing temperature and the temperature of air leaving the condenser coil.
The saturation temperature where a refrigerant blend first begins to vaporize.
Saturation temperature corresponding to head pressure from a P-T chart.
Air temperature difference between the return air entering and the supply air leaving the evaporator coil.
Return Air Temp - Supply Air Temp
The saturation temperature where a refrigerant blend first begins to condense.
Electronic gauge set that displays pressure, saturation, superheat, and subcooling values.
Actual temperature of refrigerant liquid in the liquid line at a measured point.
A chart correlating saturation pressure and temperature for a specific refrigerant.
Subtracting actual liquid line temperature from condensing saturation temperature.
Condensing Sat Temp - Liquid Line Temp
Actual temperature of refrigerant vapor in the suction line at a measured point.
Saturation temperature corresponding to suction pressure from a P-T chart.
Subtracting suction saturation temperature from actual suction line temperature.
Suction Line Temp - Suction Sat Temp
The range of temperatures over which a zeotropic blend evaporates or condenses.
Adding or removing refrigerant based on target subcooling for thermostatic expansion valves.
Adding or removing refrigerant based on target superheat for fixed orifice metering devices.
The tendency of a zeotropic blend's components to vaporize at different rates, changing liquid composition.
Air or other gases that cannot condense, raising head pressure and liquid subcooling.
Excess refrigerant in the system resulting in higher subcooling and pressure.
Desired subcooling value specified by equipment manufacturer for proper charging.
Desired superheat value based on ambient conditions and metering device type.
Insufficient refrigerant in the system resulting in low subcooling or high superheat.
Adding refrigerant until a scale shows the nameplate charge plus line set adjustment.

subjects.name: Psychrometrics
defs: The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere; standard sea level pressure is 29.92 in. Hg.
The mass of air per unit volume, typically expressed in pounds per cubic foot.
The temperature at which air becomes saturated and moisture begins to condense when cooled at constant pressure.
The temperature of air measured by a standard thermometer with a dry sensing element.
The study of the thermodynamic properties of moist air and the use of those properties to analyze air-conditioning processes.
The condition of air when it contains the maximum amount of water vapor possible at a given temperature and pressure.
The temperature at which moist air reaches saturation at a given pressure and holds the maximum water vapor possible.
The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of air by one degree Fahrenheit.
The volume occupied by a unit mass of dry air, usually expressed in cubic feet per pound of dry air.
The difference between dry-bulb temperature and wet-bulb temperature.
The temperature read by a thermometer whose bulb is covered by a wetted wick, measured in moving air.
The mass of water vapor per unit volume of moist air.
The ratio of the actual humidity ratio to the humidity ratio of saturated air at the same temperature and pressure.
The process of removing water vapor from air to lower its humidity ratio.
A unit of mass for water vapor; 7,000 grains equal 1 pound.
The process of adding water vapor to air to raise its humidity ratio.
The ratio of the mass of water vapor to the mass of dry air in a moist air mixture.
The ratio of the actual vapor pressure to the saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percent.
The partial pressure exerted by water vapor in saturated moist air at a given temperature.
The partial pressure exerted by water vapor in a moist air mixture.
A process in which air is cooled and humidified by evaporation of water with no heat exchange to the surroundings.
The ratio of sensible heat removal to total heat removal based on measured entering and leaving air conditions.
The total heat content of moist air per unit mass of dry air, including sensible and latent heat.
The ratio of sensible heat load to total heat load for a process.
The sum of sensible heat and latent heat; equivalent to enthalpy change for air-water vapor mixtures.
A vertical line on a standard psychrometric chart representing constant dry-bulb temperature.
A horizontal line on a standard psychrometric chart representing constant moisture content.
A line on the psychrometric chart representing constant total heat content of moist air.
A graphical representation of the thermodynamic properties of moist air used to analyze air-conditioning processes.
The curved line on a psychrometric chart representing 100 percent relative humidity.
A line on the psychrometric chart representing constant wet-bulb temperature.
The effective dew-point temperature of a cooling coil surface representing the condition of air leaving an ideal coil.
The fraction of air that passes through a coil without being fully conditioned.
The fraction of air that comes into contact with the coil surface and is conditioned.
Cooling air below its dew point, causing condensation and removing moisture while lowering temperature.
Adiabatic cooling process in which water is evaporated into air, lowering dry-bulb temperature and increasing humidity.
Heating air while adding moisture, typically increasing both dry-bulb temperature and humidity ratio.
The process of combining two or more air streams to form a third air stream with properties determined by mass and energy balance.
Cooling air at constant humidity ratio, resulting in a decrease in dry-bulb temperature.
Heating air at constant humidity ratio, resulting in an increase in dry-bulb temperature.
The dry-bulb temperature of air delivered from a conditioning unit into the conditioned space.

subjects.name: Electrical Controls
defs: A complete path for electric current to flow from a source through a load and back to the source.
A low current circuit that uses switches and relays to operate and sequence components in an HVAC system.
The voltage used to energize control devices such as thermostats relays and contactor coils in HVAC systems.
The supply voltage directly from the power source used to feed power circuits in most HVAC equipment.
A reduced voltage level typically used for control circuits to allow safer operation and smaller wiring.
A circuit in which components are connected across the same voltage source providing multiple paths for current.
A circuit that carries high current to operate loads such as motors or compressors in an HVAC system.
A circuit in which current flows through each component in a single path with no branching connections.
A heavy duty relay with larger contacts used to switch high current loads such as compressors or motors.
A switch that detects the presence or absence of fluid flow and opens or closes a control circuit.
A safety switch that opens a circuit when temperature or position exceeds a preset limit in an HVAC system.
A contact condition in which the circuit is closed with no power to the coil and opens when energized.
A contact condition in which the circuit is open with no power to the coil and closes when energized.
A switch that opens or closes a circuit based on system pressure to protect or control HVAC equipment.
An electromechanical device that uses a small control current to open or close one or more sets of contacts.
A manually operated switch that opens or closes a circuit by moving a lever between positions.
A single phase motor using a start capacitor in series with the start winding for high starting torque.
A combination of contactor and overload protection used to start and protect a motor from excessive current.
A protective device that opens the control circuit when motor current exceeds a safe value for a period of time.
A single phase motor with a run capacitor permanently in the circuit providing quiet operation and good efficiency.
A capacitor connected in the circuit during motor operation to improve efficiency and power factor of a motor.
A simple single phase motor with low starting torque used in small fans and light duty applications.
A single phase induction motor using a start winding and run winding with a phase shift for starting torque.
A capacitor used only during motor starting to increase starting torque then removed from the circuit.
A component in older thermostats that artificially heats or affects the sensing element to improve cycle timing.
A device in some thermostats that delays or controls cooling cycles by anticipating system operation.
The temperature difference between thermostat cut-in and cut-out points before the next heating or cooling cycle starts.
An electronic thermostat using solid state components to sense temperature and control system operation.
A small resistor in a thermostat that adds heat to the bimetal element to shorten heating cycles.
A thermostat that automatically changes temperature setpoints at different times of day to save energy.
The desired temperature value that a thermostat is set to maintain in a conditioned space.
A temperature sensing control device that opens or closes circuits to maintain a desired space temperature.
A temperature control that protects against freezing by shutting down or operating equipment at low temperatures.
A heat sensitive safety device that melts at a set temperature to open a circuit and stop equipment operation.
A temperature safety control that shuts down the heat source if furnace temperature exceeds a preset limit.
A safety control that opens the compressor circuit when refrigerant pressure exceeds a safe maximum value.
A safety control that opens the compressor circuit when refrigerant pressure falls below a safe minimum value.
A control device that regulates normal system operation based on conditions like temperature or pressure.
A safety switch that opens the burner circuit if flames roll out of a furnace combustion chamber.
A device designed to shut down or prevent operation of HVAC equipment when unsafe conditions are detected.

subjects.name: Codes and Safety
defs: Acceptable to the AHJ based on investigation, tests, or evidence demonstrating compliance with applicable codes or standards.
The organization, office, or individual responsible for enforcing codes, standards, or regulations in a given jurisdiction.
A legally adopted set of rules that establishes minimum requirements for the design, construction, installation, and alteration of buildings and systems.
A model code developed by ICC that establishes minimum regulations for mechanical systems, including HVAC, used by many US jurisdictions.
Equipment that has been evaluated by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory and found to conform to applicable product safety standards.
A widely adopted US standard (NFPA 70) for electrical wiring and equipment installation to safeguard persons and property from electrical hazards.
A documented set of criteria, methods, or practices developed by consensus that may be referenced by codes for compliance.
A refrigerant classified as mildly flammable under ASHRAE 34, requiring charge limits, ignition-source controls, and ventilation provisions during installation and service.
US EPA regulations under the Clean Air Act requiring certification for technicians who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of equipment that could release regulated refrigerants.
A dedicated space that meets ASHRAE 15 construction and ventilation requirements for refrigerant-containing equipment whose charge exceeds defined limits.
A document providing hazard information, handling precautions, first aid, exposure limits, and spill response for a specific refrigerant.
The risk that heavier-than-air refrigerants can displace oxygen in low or confined spaces, creating a suffocation hazard.
Fixed sensors that monitor a machinery room or occupied space for refrigerant concentration and trigger alarms, ventilation, or equipment shutdown at set thresholds.
Processing used refrigerant to meet ARI-700 (or equivalent) purity specifications, usually performed by a EPA-certified reclaimer off-site.
The process of removing refrigerant from a system and storing it in an approved recovery container without necessarily processing it.
Cleaning refrigerant for reuse by oil separation and single or multiple passes through filter-driers, typically done on-site with approved equipment.
Under EPA Section 608, knowingly releasing regulated refrigerants into the atmosphere during service, maintenance, repair, or disposal is prohibited except in limited, allowable cases.
A dangerous release of energy caused by an electric arc, producing intense heat, light, pressure, and risk of serious injury.
The distance from energized equipment within which a person could receive a second-degree burn from an arc flash, set by an incident energy analysis.
A device or group of devices used to disconnect equipment from its power supply, required by the NEC for service and maintenance.
The minimum unobstructed space required in front of electrical equipment for safe inspection, testing, and servicing per NEC requirements.
The intentional connection of conductive equipment parts to earth or an equipment grounding conductor to reduce shock and fire hazards.
A device that detects imbalances between hot and neutral conductors and quickly interrupts power to protect against electric shock.
OSHA-required procedures to shut off and isolate energy sources and prevent re-energization while servicing or repairing equipment.
Devices such as fuses or circuit breakers that interrupt current when it exceeds safe levels to prevent overheating or fire.
The risk posed by odorless, colorless carbon monoxide produced by incomplete combustion, which can be fatal in poorly ventilated spaces.
Air provided to fuel-burning appliances to support proper combustion and prevent negative pressure issues, as required by mechanical and fuel gas codes.
Outdoor air introduced to replace air exhausted by mechanical systems to maintain pressure balance in a building.
Ventilation provided by powered equipment, such as fans or blowers, to supply or exhaust air as required by code.
Air movement into and out of a space by natural forces such as wind or temperature difference, without powered ventilation equipment.
Air taken from outside the building envelope, used for ventilation, dilution, or combustion purposes.
The amount of outdoor air required to be provided to a space, often expressed in cubic feet per minute (cfm) per person or per unit area.
Suffocation resulting from lack of oxygen or displacement of breathable air, a risk in confined spaces or areas with heavy refrigerant leaks.
Tissue damage caused by contact with extremely cold refrigerants or surfaces, which can cause burns similar to thermal burns.
A space large enough to enter but with limited means of entry/exit and not designed for continuous occupancy, which may present atmospheric or physical hazards.
Systems or equipment, including harnesses, guardrails, or warning lines, used to prevent or arrest falls from heights.
A confined space containing a hazardous atmosphere, engulfment risk, or other serious hazard that requires a written entry permit, atmospheric testing, and an attendant.
Equipment worn by workers to minimize exposure to hazards, such as eye protection, gloves, footwear, hearing protection, or respiratory protection.
Equipment and procedures used to protect against inhalation of harmful dusts, vapors, gases, or oxygen-deficient atmospheres.
A standardized document (16 sections) that communicates chemical hazards, safe handling, PPE, and emergency procedures for a substance or mixture.
